food.text: The French introduced the baguette to Vietnam in the mid-19th century, during the Nguyễn dynasty. It became a staple food by the early 20th century. Because imported wheat was expensive, French baguettes and sandwiches were at first considered a luxury.

Under Nguyễn rule, Chinese merchants in southern Vietnam exported rice to other Southeast Asian countries and largely ignored local laws that tightly regulated such exports. Rice prices rose by 50 to 100 percent in the 1820s as a result. This irked the court of Emperor Minh Mạng.

Singapore was established as a British port in 1819. Its position as an international shipping port has exposed its cuisine to many different cultures ever since. Malay, Chinese, Indian, Peranakan and Western traditions all shaped what people eat there.

Prawn crackers are made from a dough of starch, commonly tapioca, with ground seafood and seasonings. The dough is rolled, sliced and dried, then fried, when the slices rapidly expand to a light, crisp texture. The snack is popular across Southeast Asia under names such as krupuk udang and keropok udang.

Northern Vietnamese first called the baguette bánh tây, literally "Western bánh". Southern Vietnamese called it bánh mì, meaning "wheat bánh". Nguyễn Đình Chiểu mentioned the baguette in his 1861 poem "Văn tế nghĩa sĩ Cần Giuộc".

Singapore's early immigrants adapted dishes to the ingredients and tastes available to them. Fish head curry, kaya toast and Hainanese chicken rice were created this way. They remain culinary staples in Singaporean cuisine today.

In Vietnam's Mekong Delta, rice cultivation and shrimp farming were central to local subsistence and trade. Production of the shrimp cracker bánh phồng tôm in Sa Đéc expanded during the 19th century under the Nguyễn dynasty. The crackers circulated through South China Sea trade routes.

Some dishes in Singaporean cuisine, such as laksa, biryani and betel quid, are believed to predate Raffles' arrival in 1819. Nobody knows when they reached Singapore, because early immigrants made them at home rather than serving them in an establishment. Historical records on them are scattered and inaccurate.

Commercial links maintained by Hokkien and Teochew merchants helped move shrimp-based products into Southeast Asia. In southern China, particularly Fujian and Guangdong, shrimp paste mixed with rice flour was used to make xiāpiàn. In Southeast Asia these products were adapted to local ingredients and preferences.

art.text: Yangon has the highest concentration of colonial buildings in the world. Britain made Yangon and Myanmar a colony in 1824, shortly after the First Anglo-Burmese War, and held it until independence in 1948.

The bridge designed by Gustave Eiffel was built from 1899 to 1902 and stretched 2.4 kilometres, making it the longest bridge in Asia for its time. The French built it, but most of the work was done by 3000 Vietnamese. It was formerly named Paul Doumer.

With French colonization of Vietnam in the 19th century, many French-styled buildings went up, including villas, government buildings and opera houses. Many still stand today and are among the clearest remnants of the French colonial legacy.
In 1824, the Las Piñas Bamboo Organ was created in the Philippines. It became the first and only organ made of bamboo.

Yangon's Ministers building was built between 1889 and 1905 and was designed by British architect Henry Hoyne-Fox. It covers 400,000 square feet, and its classical red brick wings, with some cast stone dressings, are arranged in a semi-circle around an inner quadrangle. It was a hub of colonial bureaucracy.

Singapore's shophouses had two stories and a long, narrow design. A canopy overhung the walkway, known as a 5-foot-way, and Sir Stamford Raffles designed them so that every house should have a verandah. The original shophouses were low, with Doric columns.

During the 19th and 20th centuries, French influence was absorbed into Vietnamese art. The liberal and modern use of color began to set Vietnamese silk paintings apart from their Chinese, Japanese and Korean counterparts. They typically show the countryside, landscapes, pagodas, historical events or scenes of daily life.

In 1884, the paintings Assassination of Governor Bustamante and His Son and Spoliarium both won prizes during an art competition in Spain. They are listed among the notable Philippine artworks of the era.
tags: Assassination of Governor Bustamante and His Son

art.text: San Sebastian Church in Manila was built in 1891. It is described as the first and only all-steel church in Asia.

In the 19th century, the Đại Estuary narrowed and the Cổ Cò River silted up, and the Nguyễn dynasty restricted Western trade. Hội An lost its role as an international port. Even so, most surviving residences and community halls there took their current architectural form during this period.
The Basi Revolt paintings were made in 1807. They depict the Ilocano revolution against Spanish interference in basi production and consumption.

Le Van Mien (1873 to 1943) likely first encountered oil painting at the school of fine arts in Paris. He returned to Hanoi in 1895, but no record shows that he taught this Western medium to craftsmen in Bien Hoa or Gia Dinh.

war.text: By the 19th century, all of Southeast Asia had been forced into European spheres of influence, with the single exception of Siam. Siam served as a convenient buffer state sandwiched between British Burma and French Indochina. Even so, its kings had to contend with repeated humiliations, accept unequal treaties amid massive French and British political interference, and suffer territorial losses.

The French conquest of Vietnam ran from 1858 to 1885 as a series of military expeditions against the Vietnamese empire of Đại Nam. France defeated the Vietnamese and their Chinese allies in 1885. It then established French Indochina over Mainland Southeast Asia in 1887.

During the British colonization of Burma in the 19th century, there was intense Buddhist militarization and resistance against the colonial occupiers. Its aim was to restore the ideal Buddhist monarchy.

A joint Franco-Spanish expedition began in 1858 by invading Tourane, modern Da Nang, in September and Saigon five months later. The four-year campaign ended when Emperor Tự Đức signed a treaty in June 1862. It gave the French sovereignty over three provinces in the South.

The French annexed the three southwestern provinces in 1867 to form Cochinchina. Having consolidated their power there, they conquered the rest of Vietnam through a series of campaigns in Tonkin between 1873 and 1886. The Qing dynasty opposed these ambitions, since it considered the region part of its sphere of influence.

In 1831 the American merchantman Friendship of Salem returned to report that it had been plundered in Sumatra, and that its first officer and two crewmen had been murdered. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 obligated the Dutch to ensure the safety of shipping and overland trade in and around Aceh, so the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army was sent on a punitive expedition in 1831.

In 1847, French Captain Lapierre sailed to Danang with two warships after Bishop Lefèbvre was arrested again. Lefèbvre was freed before things escalated, but Lapierre, unaware of this, opened fire and destroyed five Vietnamese ships in Da Nang Bay. Outraged by the attack, Emperor Thiệu Trị ordered all European documents smashed, ended all trade with France, and ordered all foreign missionaries jailed and executed.

Emperor Hàm Nghi was betrayed by a Muong chief who asked for French troops to capture him in a refugee camp in November 1888. He was deported to Algeria. Meanwhile, anti-French and anti-Catholic Cần Vương rebellions had raged across Tonkin and Annam, and more than 40,000 Catholics, 18 French missionaries and 40 Vietnamese pastors were murdered, and 9,000 churches were destroyed by angry mobs. After his capture, mandarins and members of the Cần Vương movement gradually surrendered, though a few leaders kept resisting.

President Andrew Jackson ordered America's first Sumatran punitive expedition in 1832, followed by another in 1838. The Friendship incident, in which the ship was plundered and its first officer and two crewmen murdered, gave the Dutch a reason to take over Aceh. It also let Jackson send diplomat Edmund Roberts, who secured the Roberts Treaty with Siam in 1833.

After the emperor vanished, mandarins and members of the Cần Vương movement gradually surrendered to France, but a few spearheads kept resisting. Đề Nắm was killed in 1891, Phan Đình Phùng in 1896, and Hoàng Hoa Thám in 1913. Their deaths spanned over two decades of resistance after the French conquest.

literature.text: Nguyễn Du wrote The Tale of Kiều in chữ Nôm, and it is one of the best-known pieces of Vietnamese literature. The 1820 poem is so full of obscure archaic words and Chinese borrowings that modern Vietnamese struggle to understand an alphabetic transcription without clarifications.

Although all formal writing in Vietnam was done in Classical Chinese until the early 20th century, some Vietnamese literati used chữ Nôm to create popular works in the vernacular, many in verse. The script was so complex that it was accessible only to the less than five percent of the Vietnamese population who had mastered written Chinese.
Gia Long, founder of the Nguyễn dynasty, supported chữ Nôm only for as long as it took him to become emperor. He then immediately reverted to Chinese, and his reign ran from 1802 to 1820.
Nôm was the dominant script in Vietnamese Catholic literature until the late 19th century. In 1838, Jean-Louis Taberd compiled a Nôm dictionary, which helped with the standardization of the script.
The Temple of Literature in Hanoi hosted the Imperial Academy, Vietnam's first national university, from 1076 to 1779. In 1803, the academy was moved to Hue, the new capital of the Nguyễn dynasty.

Until the 19th century, Classical Chinese was the language of formal writing in Vietnam. Popular literature and folk songs, between the 15th and 19th centuries, were written in Vietnamese using chữ Nôm, a script derived from Chinese characters. The Latin-based chữ Quốc Ngữ arrived under French rule.
Gia Long's successor Minh Mạng, the second emperor of the Nguyễn dynasty, prohibited the use of Nôm in the government. He reigned from 1820 to 1841.

The reformist Catholic scholar Nguyễn Trường Tộ presented Emperor Tự Đức with a series of unsuccessful petitions. His 1867 petition Tế cấp bát điều, or 'Eight urgent matters', proposed replacing Classical Chinese with Vietnamese written in a script he called Quốc âm Hán tự.

Built in 1805 in Hanoi's Temple of Literature, the Khuê Văn pavilion is a symbol of present-day Hanoi. Many poetic phrases preserved on the pavilion glorify Vietnamese traditional culture, and two neighboring gates are dedicated to the beauty of literature, both its content and its form.

By the 19th century, a sizable body of literature in chữ Nôm had accumulated. Because it served as a written medium for oral dissemination, individuals in villages could pass these texts on by speaking them aloud.

Nguyễn Trường Tộ's petitions to Emperor Tự Đức were written in Classical Chinese, like all court documents, even though they argued for change. One section was titled Xin khoan dung quốc âm, meaning 'Please tolerate the national voice'. He described his proposed script as a new creation and did not mention chữ Nôm.

science.text: In 1868, young Chulalongkorn traveled with his father, King Mongkut, to Prachuap Khiri Khan Province to observe the solar eclipse of 18 August 1868. Both father and son contracted malaria on the trip. Mongkut, who had proved correct in his eclipse predictions, died of the illness in Bangkok on October 1, 1868, and Chulalongkorn, only 15, was chosen king by a council.

By the late 19th century, Dutch growers were cultivating cinchona trees on plantations across the Indonesian islands. Cinchona bark was used to make quinine, a drug for treating malaria, and the Dutch soon became the main suppliers of it.

The Tonkin Free School was founded in March 1907 in Hanoi. It offered free evening classes in modern subjects such as science, hygiene and French, aiming to modernize Vietnamese society under the French protectorate.

During his 1897 tour of Europe, Chulalongkorn spent much time in Britain. He was inspired there to improve the health of the Siamese people by creating public health, or sanitary, districts back home in Siam.
During his 1897 tour of Europe, Chulalongkorn visited Sweden. There he studied the country's forestry system, one of many practical subjects he examined as part of his broader modernization of Siam.

In 1907, Chulalongkorn visited his son's school in Britain. While there, he consulted with European doctors in pursuit of a cure for his kidney disease. The treatment did not save him: he died of kidney disease on 23 October 1910 at the Amphorn Sathan Residential Hall in the Dusit Palace.
In 1913, the future Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences began as a department of the Royal Medical College at Siriraj Hospital. It would be years before it became an independent faculty.

politics.text: By the 19th century, all of Southeast Asia had been forced into European spheres of influence except Siam. It served as a convenient buffer state sandwiched between British Burma and French Indochina.

The Nguyễn dynasty was the last Vietnamese dynasty. It ruled a unified Vietnam independently from 1802 until the start of the French protectorate in 1883, and its emperors were members of the House of Nguyễn Phúc.

France absorbed the Nguyễn dynasty gradually over several decades. It began with the Cochinchina Campaign in 1858, which led to the occupation of southern Vietnam, and a series of unequal treaties followed.

Vietnamese territory was carved up by treaty. The 1862 Treaty of Saigon made the occupied south the French colony of Cochinchina, and the 1863 Treaty of Huế gave France access to Vietnamese ports and increased control of its foreign affairs.

In 1887, Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin, and the French Protectorate of Cambodia were grouped together to form French Indochina. The Nguyễn Phúc rulers kept only nominal rule over the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin.

Siam's kings had to accept unequal treaties amid heavy French and British political interference. They also suffered territorial losses after the Franco-Siamese crisis of 1893 and the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909.

In 1913, Dutch cinchona growers in Indonesia set up the Kina Bureau. This cartel was charged with controlling the price and production of quinine, the drug made from cinchona bark used to treat malaria.

The Tonkin Free School operated legally for several months before French authorities shut it down that November. After a 1908 tax revolt in Annam and a poisoning attempt on French soldiers in Hanoi were blamed on its leaders, they were arrested and its publications were suppressed.

After the 1862 Treaty of Saigon, and especially after France completely conquered Lower Cochinchina in 1867, the Văn Thân movement of the scholar-gentry class arose. It committed violence against Catholics across central and northern Vietnam. Later, during the early colonial period, guerrillas of the royalist Cần Vương movement massacred around a third of Vietnam's Christian population, and anti-Catholic violence persisted in Nam Định, Quảng Trị and Bình Định during the 1880s.

Emperor Minh Mạng introduced new measures to curb Chinese trade from 1831 onwards, beginning with restrictions banning residents from overseas travel. These culminated in a brief revolt among the residents of Gia Dinh in 1833. Lê Văn Duyệt had noticed the Chinese held great autonomy over trade affairs there.

Hội An declined as an international port in the 19th century, when silting of the Cổ Cò River prevented large ships from docking. The Nguyễn dynasty's isolationist policies restricting Western trade diminished its role further. In 1888, Đà Nẵng became a French concession and many Chinese merchants relocated there.

In 1847 French Captain Lapierre, unaware that the imprisoned bishop Dominique Lefèbvre had already been freed, opened fire and destroyed five Vietnamese ships in Da Nang Bay. Outraged, Emperor Thiệu Trị ordered all European documents smashed, all trade and terms with France ended, and all foreign missionaries jailed and executed. The persecution of Catholics had already been under way since 1833, with French bishops among those put to death.

The 1883 Treaty of Huế turned the rest of Vietnam into the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin. French diplomatic circles considered its terms overly harsh and never ratified it in France, so the 1884 Treaty of Huế softened it.

In 1833 the United States secured the Roberts Treaty with Siam through diplomat Edmund Roberts, dispatched by President Andrew Jackson. When the treaty was renegotiated in 1856, Townsend Harris told Siam that the United States held no possessions in the East and did not desire any.

Emperor Minh Mạng grew irked when Chinese traders ignored rice export rules, which pushed rice prices up 50 to 100 percent in the 1820s. From 1831 he introduced measures to curb Chinese trade, including bans on overseas travel, which culminated in a brief revolt in Gia Dinh in 1833.

After French ships destroyed five Vietnamese ships in Da Nang Bay in 1847, an outraged Emperor Thiệu Trị ordered all European documents smashed and all foreign missionaries jailed and executed. His son Tự Đức renewed the persecution of Catholics, and in 1857 he executed two Spanish Dominican priests, which led France and Spain to declare war.

The Salem merchantman Friendship returned in 1831 to report that it had been plundered in Sumatra and that its first officer and two crewmen had been murdered. This gave the Dutch a reason to take over Aceh. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 had obligated them to ensure the safety of shipping there, so they sent a punitive expedition in 1831, and America's own followed in 1832.

philosophy.text: The advent of the steamship in the 19th century made the Hajj easier for Muslims in Southeast Asia. As pilgrimage grew more popular, Arabic and the Arabian brand of Islam were integrated further into their lives.

Under French rule in Vietnam, a Western-style system of modern education introduced new humanist values. This came as the French administration imposed significant political and cultural changes on Vietnamese society after Vietnam was integrated into French Indochina in 1887.

The mystic Đoàn Minh Huyên (1807–1856) practiced Đạo Bửu Sơn Kỳ Hương, or the Way of the Strange Fragrance from the Precious Mountain, which blended Buddhist, Taoist, Confucian and Zen elements. He claimed to be a living Buddha in the Thất Sơn range on the Vietnamese-Cambodian border. During a cholera epidemic in 1849 that killed over a million people, Huyên was reputed to have supernatural abilities to cure the sick and the insane, and his followers wore amulets bearing the Chinese characters for Bửu Sơn Kỳ Hương.

Emperor Tự Đức, aware of the rise of Western influences in Asia, reannounced Vietnam's isolationist closed country policy. He welcomed no French, British, American or Spanish embassies, increased the prohibition of trade, and renewed the persecution of Catholics. In 1857 he executed two Spanish Dominican priests, and France and Spain declared war and launched the invasion of Vietnam.

A mass migration of Chinese into Malaysia began in the 19th century, driven by the tin and gold mining days. The migrants built temples for their deities, along with schools and cemeteries. Mining created a need for temples for religious rituals.
philosophy.source_title: Chinese folk religion in Southeast Asia

philosophy.text: During the French colonial period, Catholicism and a Latin script romanizing Vietnamese, the chữ Quốc Ngữ, were introduced in Vietnam. Until the 19th century, Classical Chinese had been the language used for formal writing.
During the Nguyễn dynasty's persecution of Catholics in Vietnam, non-Catholics were called lương dân. The terms bên lương and bên giáo were used to tell non-Catholic and Catholic sides apart.

culture.text: The name Indochina was coined in the early nineteenth century by outsiders. It stressed the long cultural influence of Indian and Chinese civilizations on the region. The French later adopted it as the name of their colony of French Indochina.
The French colonial period brought Catholicism to Vietnam. It also brought a Latin script for writing Vietnamese, the Vietnamese alphabet, called chữ Quốc Ngữ, or 'National Language Script'.

French rule imposed significant political and cultural changes on Vietnamese society. A Western-style system of modern education introduced new humanist values. Most French settlers lived in Cochinchina, particularly Saigon, and in Hanoi, the colony's capital.

The name Indo-China is usually credited to two Europeans. The Danish-French geographer Conrad Malte-Brun wrote of the area as indo-chinois in 1804. The Scottish linguist John Leyden used Indo-Chinese for its inhabitants and their languages in 1808.

In the 19th century the islands of Maritime Southeast Asia were also known by the term Malay Archipelago. It followed the 16th-century term East Indies. Arab merchants and cartographers had called the region the Java archipelago, and its people 'Al-Jawi'.
The Nguyễn court experimented with ways to assimilate Chinese immigrants. In 1839 an edict abolished the Chinese clan associations in Vietnamese-ruled Cambodia, but it proved ineffective.

Europeans thought the mainland had a dual Indian and Chinese makeup. In reality it held about 12 different kingdoms and other territories, with a population descended from 23 different societies. The French failed to recognize this diversity and simply called the region Indochina.

Emperor Thiệu Trị allowed only Chinese-born immigrants to register with the Chinese clan associations. Their local-born male descendants could register with the Minh-Huong-xa and adorn the Vietnamese costume, so clothing became a sign of belonging.
